title: When Union and State laws clash, the Union usually wins. Usually.
sources: Constitution of India, Articles 246, 248, 254 and 356; Seventh Schedule
S. R. Bommai v. Union of India, Supreme Court, 1994 (nine-judge bench)

quiz.q: Who holds powers over subjects on no list?
quiz.why: Right. Article 248 gives Parliament exclusive power over any matter not in the State or Concurrent List (residuary powers).

script: When a Union law and a State law clash, the Union usually wins.
Usually.
Article 246 splits law-making into three lists:
Article two forty-six splits law-making into three lists:
Union, State, and Concurrent.
A subject on no list belongs to Parliament, under Article 248.
A subject on no list belongs to Parliament, under Article two forty-eight.
If a State law clashes with Parliament's law on a Concurrent subject,
the State law is void to that extent.
Unless the President assents to it.
Then it prevails in that State,
until Parliament legislates again.
And Article 356, President's Rule?
And Article three fifty-six, President's Rule?
In Bommai, in 1994, nine judges made it open to judicial review,
In Bommai, in nineteen ninety-four, nine judges made it open to judicial review,
with majority tested on the floor.
The lists divide power.
The courts guard the balance.
Your turn.

scenes.heading: Article 254: a clash on a Concurrent subject

steps.text: State law void to that extent

scenes.sub: S. R. Bommai, 1994: nine judges; majority tested on the floor

claims.claim: Article 246 and the Seventh Schedule divide subjects into the Union, State and Concurrent Lists
Article 248: Parliament has exclusive power over any matter not enumerated in the State or Concurrent List (residuary powers)
Article 254(1): a State law repugnant to a Parliament law on a Concurrent matter is void to the extent of the repugnancy
claims.quote: shall, to the extent of the repugnancy, be void

claims.claim: Article 254(2): a State law reserved for the President and assented prevails in that State; Parliament may later amend or repeal it
S. R. Bommai (1994), nine-judge bench: Article 356 proclamations are subject to judicial review; majority must be tested on the floor of the House (246, 248, 254, 356)

review_note: Constitution text read via constitutionofindia.net and two explainers, not the official Gazette copy. Simplification: Article 254(1) also covers conflicts with Union List laws; the script frames it for Concurrent subjects, where 254(2) applies. Entry counts of each list are deliberately left out (sources disagree after amendments). Episode 8 already covers Bommai in depth, so it gets one line here. Title is a framing; accurate to Art. 254(2).
